blocks.c: Chapter Nineteen: The Cracked Bell
They rang eleven double rounds over nine days and every one of them worked, and that is why nobody was ready.

You get used to things. That is the whole of it. By the fourth crossing the double round had a rota; by the sixth it had a shorthand; by the ninth, Cook Anselm was sending a hamper down on the Sprat because someone had mentioned that there were children on the platform who had never eaten an orange, and the whole business had acquired the awful comfortable feeling of a thing that is simply how it is done now.
Sol had even begun to be bored during the descent, which she recognised, in retrospect, as the exact moment the trade stops keeping you alive.
There had been warnings. There are always warnings; the trouble is that a warning and a nothing look identical until afterwards.

items: On the seventh round the Ninth's tail had come back a hair short, and Sol had marked it thin and rung again and got it full and thought no more about it.

On the ninth, Roake had run her thumb round the crown after the round and stood there with her head on one side for four seconds longer than usual, and had said nothing, because there was nothing to say that a tally would accept.

On the tenth, Dov had reported a change in the frame note under load and had written it up and filed it, and it had gone into the pile of things to look at in Antrell, along with a sticking valve and a door that would not shut.

blocks.c: Nobody was careless. That is the part Sol needed people to understand afterwards, and never once managed to say without sounding as though she were making excuses. A bell of forty-one years that has been rung four times a day at an interval a tenth of a beat wrong has been very slightly hurt on every single one of those strikes, sixty thousand times, and then one day it is rung correctly and the correct blow is the one that finds the fault.
They had fixed the count. The count was what killed it.
On the eleventh, coming up on the Quiet in a wind off the north with a squall line running ahead of it, the Ninth cracked.

It did not shatter. Bells almost never do. What happened was that Roake struck a true blow on a bell that had been rung four times a day for eleven years with a tenth of a beat missing from its count, and forty-one years of stress in the crown found a fault the size of a hair and travelled eleven inches along it in about a thousandth of a second.

The sound it made was not loud. It was worse than loud. It was a note that started and then went wrong in the middle, a bright ringing thing turning into a flat, buzzing, meat-like noise, and Sol, with her hand on the frame, felt the carry go out from under the whole ship like a floor being taken away.
"Off!" Roake screamed. "Hammer off! Nobody strike it!"
The Gull went down eleven spans in nineteen seconds.
What that is like is this.

The lamps swing and the shadows all run one way. The deck is not soft now; the deck is gone, and you are standing on a thing that is falling at the same speed you are, which is the definition of a floor you cannot use. Somewhere below there is the noise of four hundred and eleven people all being frightened in one place, which is a sound no one who has heard it ever describes properly.

Sol was on her knees with her fingers through the frame grating. Dov was hanging off the ballast lever with both feet off the deck. Roake was already at Keel with the hammer up, ringing the fall-off — Keel, Mother, Widow, four beats, four beats — and the three deep bells were doing what three deep bells can do, which is not enough.
"Eight bells won't hold her!" Dov shouted. "We're eleven under and the frames are cold!"
"Then get me the ninth!" Roake shouted back.
"It's cracked!"
"I know it's cracked!"

And then, in the middle of that, from below the keel line, from four hundred feet down in the dark where a nineteen-year-old with a repeater and a bell had just heard his ship's ninth bell die: the twin.

It rang alone. Out of round, out of sequence, against every rule in the trade — a bell struck by itself with nothing to lean on — and Sol felt the pull come up through the deck and turn, unmistakably, into a push.
"He's giving it back," she said.
"What?"
"Pel. He's ringing the tenth to hold us. He's spending their carry on us."
Roake's head came round.
"How long can he hold it?"
Sol did the sum with a mouth that had gone completely dry.
"Until their frame goes," she said.

And then, because there was no time to be gentle about it: "Bosun, he's nineteen and he's alone in a bell-house and he can feel our carry through the plinth. He knows exactly what he's doing and he'll do it until the platform goes soft under him, because he can hear four hundred and eleven people up here and he cannot hear two hundred and eleven behind him, and that is how anybody makes that decision."
Roake shut her eyes for precisely one beat.
"Then we take it back off him," she said, "before he gives us all of it."
"With what? We've got eight bells and a cracked ninth."
"We have got eight bells, a cracked ninth, and a hush." Roake was already moving down the line. "Get it."
